placement.position_note: PARTY-LINE FRONTAGE, DERIVED FROM THE COMMITTED PLAT (T-0078). This building does not stand centred on a lot at a typology setback: it stands ON the north face of blk_south_water_franklin, the block's South Water Street frontage, whose line and bearing are read from the block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json — the same committed geometry the lot grid and the corridor gate are derived from. Its front wall is 1.50 m back from that lot line, which is the closest line the plat module's own margin allows and is not a measurement of this frontage, and its east wall is fixed by the east end of the run's own frontage, 1.5 m clear of the side lot line at that end. The bearing is the face's own, so the front looks square at South Water Street. The run carries no lateral offset, because a shared party wall is one wall and cannot wander. WHAT IS INVENTED IS STILL EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS: that a building stood here at all, which building it was, and that these particular units stood shoulder to shoulder. What the 1834 South Water Street view supports is the TREATMENT — a continuous working row of party walls rather than detached cottages set back on grass. The treatment is what this placement takes from it, and a run standing on any other face of the town is borrowing it from that one street: the view draws a row, it does not place this row. Standing on a derived block face is not standing on a recovered lot, and the side lot lines this row crosses were always conjectural.

siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this roof wears 5.5 in — dealt in this building's own parcel recipe: drawn on this record's stable key from the stocks its household class may hang (5 in, 5.5 in or 6 in; T-1839, docs/LIBERTIES.md L352), then advanced within them so that no roof of the parcel standing within 60 m hangs the same course. It is NOT keyed to a construction season the way the named buildings' stocks are: this record's 1835-01-01 is the programme's count-unit convention and not a date anything was built, so keying to it would deal every anonymous roof in the town one stock. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention and the recipe half is recorded beside it, under `tools/siding_stock.py`.

occupants.note: SEATED BY THE PLACEMENT POLICY'S PLATTED DEAL (data/reconstruction/1835_platted_seats.json, dealt by T-1613 and carried onto this roof by T-1638; liberties L270 and L276). NO SOURCE PLACES THIS HOUSEHOLD HERE, OR ANYWHERE. Its own record gives a name and no address — no street, no lot and not even a division — so both halves of its band were dealt rather than read, and the lot under this roof is the policy's tradesman_dwellings clause answered on the committed plat: blk_south_water_franklin#04, fronting south_water, a standing roof of family D4 the clause admits. THE SOURCES BELOW CARRY THE NAME AND NOTHING ELSE. The roof's own existence, position and footprint remain conjectural and are unchanged by the seating — it is still a count-unit of the 665-roof programme, adopted rather than raised, so nothing was drawn off the reconstruction order book. The household's id is carried in resident_assignment rather than in this prose, because tools/generate_dooryard_pickets.py admits a lot for a garden on an id appearing HERE and a keeper a policy deal seats is not a measurement of anybody's garden.

what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.
Thirty-five architectural family definitions with dimensional and massing bands.
District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.

Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.

citations.citation: The first Chicago Catholic church register — Father John Mary Irenaeus St. Cyr's marriage register and his death and burial page — as printed and annotated in the *Illinois Catholic Historical Review*, vol. 4 (July 1921 - April 1922), and republished in two pages by the Genealogy Trails Transcription Team. 128 dated marriages of 1834-1839, each naming groom, bride, witnesses and officiating priest, and 11 deaths and burials of June 1834 to March 1837.

transcribes.work: The first Chicago Catholic church record, kept by Father J. M. I. St. Cyr from 1833 and continued by Fathers Bernard Schaeffer and Timothy O'Meara to 1839
transcribes.note: THE ORIGINAL, and nobody in this project has seen it. What is read here is a 1921-22 article that prints the marriage entries and the death entries and comments on them. The article itself says the death record 'is contained on a single page' of the book.

transcribes.work: Illinois Catholic Historical Review, vol. 4 (July 1921 - April 1922)
transcribes.note: The layer actually read, at one further remove: the Genealogy Trails team transcribed these two pages out of the Review and this project read the transcription. Every record citing this source is graded transcription_mediated, twice over.

what_it_supplies: 128 marriages at Chicago (125 of them) between 1834 and 1839, each dated, and each naming its witnesses BY NAME — 513 named readings of people standing at a named place on a named day
six marriages IN THE SCENE YEAR, which with their witnesses put twenty named people in Chicago on five days of 1835
eleven deaths and burials, four of them in 1835, including the death of Thomas Owen, agent of the Indians, at Chicago on 15 October 1835
the register's own arithmetic — 22 St. Cyr marriages, 18 Schaeffer, 87 O'Meara, 1 Plunkett — which verifies any reading of it without the book
the dates bounding each priest's time at Chicago, which is what makes an unsigned entry attributable
the Irish, French and German Catholic population of the town, which is the part the poll books and letter lists reach least well
what_it_does_not_supply: any address, lot, dwelling or workplace — the register places nobody anywhere in the town
any age, except for three infants and one nine-year-old on the death page
the baptisms. The article tallies 282 of them by these same priests and prints none; that register is T-0503's object and is not in this source
residence. A marriage at Chicago on a day of 1835 is presence on that day, and presence is not residence
reliable spelling. The article says so itself: a French and German priest writing Irish and English names, and an Irish priest writing French and German ones

citations.citation: The baptismal register of St Mary's, Chicago — the first Catholic parish in the town — opened by Father John Mary Irenaeus St. Cyr on 22 May 1833 and read here for the years 1833, 1834 and 1835: 57 entries in French and English naming children, parents, godparents and witnesses, with the priest's own signature under every one and eight autographs of the town's own people beside them.

transcribes.work: The baptismal register kept at Chicago by Father J. M. I. St. Cyr from May 1833
transcribes.note: THE ORIGINAL, and these eleven images are photographs of it. A reading made off them is scan_verified — the higher of this project's two reading grades — and it outranks the marriage and death pages of st_cyr_register_ichr_v4, which reached this project through a 1921-22 article and a web transcription.

what_it_supplies: 57 dated baptisms of 1833-1835 and 267 named readings of people — 46 of the entries at Chicago and 166 of the readings adults there
KINSHIP, which no other source this project holds gives at all: a child, its two parents and its two godparents on one dated line, 44 times over
the town's Catholic population — French, Métis, Irish and German — of whom 85 distinct adults reach no surname in the residents layer

eight AUTOGRAPHS: Mark Beaubien, Josette Laframboise, Augustin Bonné, Monique Nadeau, Jean Baptiste Lavigne, J. B. Beaubien, Robert A. Kinzie and Gwinthlean Whistler signing under the priest, each placing a named person at a named place on a named day in their own hand
two adult baptisms with AGES — Josette Laframboise Beaubien at 38 in June 1834 and Geneviève Medera at about 20 in June 1835 — which are the only ages this project has for either woman
the parish's own start date, 22 May 1833, on a page the book heads '1er Page'
the register's own arithmetic: pencil tallies of 19, 24 and 14 baptisms for 1833, 1834 and 1835, which check any reading of it
a hue and cry on the title page describing what a young man of the Illinois country wore in 1833 or 1834 — a white pea coat, gray pants and a fur cap
what_it_does_not_supply: any address, lot, street, dwelling or workplace — the register places nobody anywhere in the town, and names no church building on any of the eleven pages
residence, and this is the trap. A baptism documents a person at a font on a day. Presence is not residence and nothing here mints or regrades a resident
presence on 1 July 1835 for anyone not baptised or standing as sponsor within days of it
occupation. One entry writes 'Doctor Egan' — a title inside a name — and that is the only trade the book ever states

ALL CHICAGO. Entries 1-11 of 1834 were written at Bear Creek, the South Fork of the Sangamon and Springfield, in Sangamon County, on the priest's journey back from St. Louis. A reader who takes the book as a Chicago roll plants eleven households in the wrong county
reliable spelling. A French priest wrote Irish, English and German names and phoneticised Potawatomi and Odawa ones; the same woman is Nadeau, Nodeau and Nodou in his own hand on three pages
the sponsors of 1834 entry 4, which stood on a line the scan's frame cuts off
anything about 1836 or later. The two page-sides in the deposit that carry 1837-38 and 1849 entries are declared and not transcribed

frontage.why: T-1622, the third deal on this block and the one that spends its last free business-front lot. THE FACE IS NOT RE-ARGUED: this block's north face is South Water Street, the town's business front, graded `principal` in the committed hierarchy, and the two runs already standing on this block — the first deal's on lot 6 and the second's on lot 2 — stand on its line at a 1.5 m setback. This run adopts the same setback, which is what puts its front wall on the line the block's other nine frontage roofs already stand on rather than on a line of its own. LOT 4 CAME OFF TWO OPEN-LOT LISTS TO BE DEALT THIS RUN, AND NEITHER OF THEM CALLED IT A RESERVED VACANCY. The first deal declared lots 4 and 6 as its frontage and stood its whole run on lot 6; T-1053 then listed lot 4 open, saying in its own words that it was held on the list "only because this parcel's privy stood in its yard" and that the privy had since moved to the lot it serves. The second deal repeated the listing with the same reason and added the only one it had of its own: "this deal was dealt the roofs it has built and asks the block for no more ground, so the lot stays open." Neither is the end-rule reading that makes lot 1 the block's open lot; both are a parcel saying it had no roof to put there. This deal has two, and they are two the platted seating asked this block for by name. So lot 4 leaves both lists and is built on, and lot 1 — the remotest lot from the bridge and the one the schedule's sizing reserves — is still open, which is the standard the density rule actually states. THE GROUND WAS MEASURED BEFORE IT WAS DEALT. Lot 4 projects onto the north face between 47.06 m and 72.12 m, so with the plat module's 1.5 m side margin the run has 22.06 m of buildable face. The nearest roof west of it is the second deal's two-room cottage recon_1835_blk_south_water_franklin_c2_08, whose east wall reads 46.21 m; the nearest east is the first deal's log dwelling recon_1835_blk_south_water_franklin_d1_04 at 77.13 m. Neither is touched: the run is anchored at the EAST end of its own frontage at the 1.5 m margin and packs back west, which leaves 6.51 m to d1_04 and better than eleven metres to d4_08, against a three-metre separation gate.
